text.en: Your class wants a picnic but cannot agree on where to go. The teacher asks everyone to raise a hand for a choice, and the place with more hands wins. Everyone had a say in the decision. This is democracy in a small form. In this chapter we ask why we need rules and a government and how democracy works.

Human beings have lived in communities for a long time. At home, in school and at work there are rules that people follow, and employers too must follow rules. Without rules a society could not function. The group of individuals or the system that makes the rules and ensures they are followed is called a government. Rules and laws are not fixed once and for all. They can change as society changes, for example when digital technology brings new crimes such as stealing money online.
A government has three organs. The legislature is the assembly of representatives that makes new laws. The executive carries out the laws and runs the administration. The judiciary, made of courts, settles disputes and punishes those who break the law. They are kept separate but they work together. For example, if a cybercriminal steals money, the legislature has made the law against it, the police and other officers of the executive catch the offender and the court of the judiciary tries and convicts the person. This is called a system of checks and balances. If all three organs were under one group, there could be disorder and misuse of power.
A democratic government works at several levels: the Centre or national level, the State level and the local level. If a bulb at home does not light, you first check the bulb, then the switch, then the fuse. In the same way a problem is dealt with first at the level where it arises. A flood in one part of a district is handled locally. If many towns and villages are affected the State government steps in with rescue teams. Some matters, like currency and communications, are handled by the Central government, while many others are looked after by the State government and local bodies. Many institutions have mottos from ancient texts. The Supreme Court's motto is Yato Dharmastato Jayah, meaning where there is dharma, there is victory.
In a democracy the people choose their government. In many schools a class monitor is elected by the whole class. The same principle applies at the State and national levels: people vote for representatives, who become members of the assemblies. Members discuss laws and problems in assemblies and try through dialogue and debate to convince each other. In direct democracy every person takes part in the decision, as in the class vote on the picnic. In representative democracy people elect representatives who decide for them. India is the world's largest democracy, with about 970 million voters in 2024. Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, the 11th President of India, showed how a head of state who has mostly a nominal role can still inspire millions.

problem.en: Match each function with an organ: making laws, catching a thief, deciding a dispute.

text.en: Making laws is done by the legislature.
Catching a thief is the work of the executive, such as the police.
Deciding a dispute is done by the judiciary, the courts.

prompt.en: Explain the three organs and why they are kept separate.

requiredIdeas.en: Legislature makes laws, executive implements them, judiciary interprets them.
No single group can misuse power.

points.en: A government makes and enforces rules.
The three organs are legislature, executive and judiciary.
Government works at Centre, State and local levels.
In a democracy people choose their representatives by voting.
